description:
Default Orbit is a multidisciplinary team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Combining expertise in full-stack development, web development, computer science, and graphic design, we aim to build innovative solutions through collaboration, creativity, and technology.

For this challenge, we are tackling “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots”, exploring ways to improve the integration and interpretation of satellite-based fire detection data.
summary:
Museum of Fires is a web app that turns more than 25 years of NASA FIRMS fire detections (MODIS and VIIRS) into one consistent fire history, so anyone can explore how fire behaves in a place and time of year. The idea is global. For this hackathon we built the working prototype and its mock data on Argentina only. The guiding question is “is this fire normal for this place and this time of year?”
It harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS so the sensor that made a detection stops mattering.
MODIS is the reference scale. VIIRS is multiplied by a calibration factor k for each constellation regime, and for each calendar month.
k is computed only from months where every expected satellite is present.
The app adds a burning-activity calendar from 2000, region and date-range selection, downloads, and a comparison of the current month against the historical median.
MODIS is nearing the end of its life and VIIRS is replacing it, but their records aren’t directly comparable.
VIIRS also changed from one to three satellites and back to two (S-NPP stopped delivering on 2 November 2026). That creates fake jumps in fire counts.
Without harmonization, nobody has a consistent picture of when and where land burned.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

A Python pipeline (FIRMS archive plus near-real-time data) aggregates detections into H3 cell-days, calibrates k, validates it and exports versioned artifacts.

A Next.js web app reads those artifacts and offers:

History: the harmonized calendar.

Map: a fire globe.

Today: an anomaly view against the baseline.

Method: how the harmonization works.

Fire museum: a curated set of historical fires, each cross-checked against FIRMS detections by latitude/longitude and dates.

The prototype data covers Argentina, with 8 museum events. The pipeline and method don’t depend on the country, so extending to other regions means loading their FIRMS data.

The main benefit is educational. Students, teachers and the public can see how fire seasons, anomalies and big historical fires look in real satellite data.

They also see why different satellites need to be harmonized, and how scientists validate that.

The museum tells each story with sources, so people learn from real events and not just charts.

What is the expected impact?

It makes fire history easier to understand and teach, and it gives the public a consistent baseline across the MODIS-to-VIIRS transition.

Because the method is not country-specific, it can scale to any region.

This is a projection. No school, agency or user has validated the tool yet.

What tools did you use?

Data: NASA FIRMS (yearly CSVs and the area API).

Pipeline: Python 3.12, DuckDB, H3, uv, pytest, ruff.

Web: Next.js 16, TypeScript, globe.gl, h3-js, Leaflet, hosted on Vercel.

Museum research: Tavily searches, reviewed by a person.

AI applied: Claude Code, Codex and Gemini.

How is it creative?

The correction is explicit and per regime and calendar month, because k turned out to be seasonal.

A simulated S-NPP drop estimates k for the current two-satellite regime, which never had a standard product.

The Museum of Fires places the harmonized series next to real historical fires.

The story hooks are “the same fire seen by MODIS with X detections and by VIIRS with 2X” and “the satellite that died 12 days ago”.

What factors did your team consider?

Time: the deadline is 23:59 on 15 November, so the plan is core-first and the extras were cut.

Validity: the holdout monthly MAPE is 19.3%, down from 35.8% with a single k.

Accessibility: color-blind-safe color ramps, with values also shown as text.

Scalability: the method and pipeline are not specific to one country. Only the mock data is Argentina-only, so other regions can be added by loading their FIRMS data.

Limitations stated openly:

Data is Argentina-only for now.

2026 still runs above MODIS.

The provisional months (August to November 2026) are worse.

k is national.

The Terra-only period (2000–2002) isn’t corrected.
